notes.meaning: God rejects people who wander away from His laws and live by their own rules. Their clever tricks and lies are empty and come to nothing. In fact, the traps they set for others end up bringing ruin on themselves.

Dross is the scum skimmed off the top of melting metal and thrown away. In God's eyes the wicked are like that: worthless, with no true metal in them. One day He will separate them from His people. Seeing where sin leads makes the writer love God's word even more, because it warns him away from that road.

The word for "trembles" pictures his skin shuddering and his hair standing on end. He does not gloat over the wicked when they fall. Instead he is humbled and stands in awe of God. This holy fear sits alongside his love for God. Thinking about his own weakness, it turns him back to God (what the Bible calls repentance).

The writer can honestly say he has treated people fairly and given everyone their due. Still, he has enemies, so he asks God not to leave him in their hands. A "surety" is someone who stands in for another person as their guarantee. He asks God to step between him and the proud people who oppress him. Matthew Henry adds that Christ is our surety before God.

He has watched so long for God's help that his eyes feel worn out. Help seems slow in coming. Yet he waits for God's promise, which is righteous and so cannot fail. His eyes may grow tired, but God's word does not.

He asks God to treat him by His mercy and faithful love, not by what he deserves. He calls himself God's servant. He is not boasting. He is reminding God that he belongs to Him. A servant needs his master to show him the work, so he asks God for understanding to know His word. Anyone who truly wants to do God's will shall come to know it.

People have openly thrown off God's law as if it did not count. The writer says it is time for the LORD to step in and hold back evil. When the wicked have made a total mess of things, that is God's time to help. Matthew Henry notes the words can also mean "it is time to work for the LORD." We do what we can for Him, then ask Him to take the work into His own hands.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Keil and Delitzsch prefer the reading "it is time to act for the LORD." They see it as a call for God's people to act, not a call for God to judge.

notes.meaning: Because others reject God's law, the writer holds it even closer. He loves it more than the purest gold. Gold cannot make the soul rich toward God, but God's word can. He counts every one of God's commands as right. He hates every false way, because sin runs against what God says.

God's word is full of wonders: deep mysteries, wise directions and great promises. These things are far above everyday human thinking. So the writer keeps them like treasure in his soul. He studies them carefully until he understands.

"Unfolding" means opening up or explaining God's word, like opening a door to let light in. God Himself opens His word to those who want to learn. His Spirit uses it to bring light to the mind. Even "the simple," meaning plain or inexperienced people, gain real understanding from it.

He pictures himself with his mouth open, panting. He is like a traveler in a hot desert gasping for a cool breeze, or an animal worn out from a chase. That is how strongly he longs for God's word. Our longing for God should be just as earnest.

It is a humble prayer. He asks God to look on him kindly and show mercy. He does not claim to have earned it. He simply asks to be treated the way God always treats His friends, those who love His name.

He asks God to make his steps firm and steady, guided by His word. We must ask God's Spirit to direct how we walk. He also prays that no sin will rule him, especially the sin of turning away from God under pressure. God's promise answers this prayer: sin shall not be your master (Romans 6:14).

"Redeem" here means rescue. He asks God to free him from cruel people, who are only human and whose power God can limit. He would keep obeying God even while oppressed. But once set free, he could serve God more gladly and freely.

Asking God to make His face shine means asking for His smile and approval. The writer wants to know he is accepted by God, even if the world frowns on him. He also asks to be taught God's ways. We should pray for grace to obey as earnestly as we pray for comfort.

He weeps rivers of tears because people do not keep God's law. His grief is not about his own troubles. It is for God's honor and for the harm sinners bring on themselves. His sorrow is like Jeremiah's. We should grieve over what we cannot fix.

God is completely good and right in who He is. So everything He decides and does is right as well. He never has done wrong to anyone, and He never can. His commands come from His holiness and from His honest care for people's good. They are fully trustworthy.

Zeal is a burning concern for God's honor. Seeing his enemies push God's words out of their minds wore him out, body and spirit. What grieved him was not wrongs done to him, but God being dishonored. Matthew Henry compares this to Jesus' zeal for God's house (John 2:17). Such zeal should move us to do what we can against sin, or at least to live better ourselves.
God's promise is like metal refined in fire and proven pure. There is no trace of falsehood in it. The writer loves it because it reflects God's holiness. Taken to heart, it also purifies us.
He feels small and looked down on, yet he does not forget God's commands. Hard times are the true test of faith. When we feel small and despised, we need God's word all the more to hold us up.

other.label: Catholic and Orthodox
other.view: The ancient Greek and Latin Bibles, long used in Orthodox and Catholic churches, read "I am young" instead of "I am lowly."

notes.meaning: God's righteousness never changes. It is the same in every age and place. His law is true, so it can never mislead us about His promises. Matthew Henry adds that the law shows what is holy, but only Christ's obedience justifies a believer, which means makes them right with God.

Trouble from outside and anguish inside have gripped him. Yet God's commands are still his joy, and believers often taste that joy most in hard times. God's word is right forever. He asks for understanding so that he may truly live. Knowing God is eternal life (John 17:3), and life without knowing God is a kind of death.

He prays with his whole heart, not just his lips. Prayer counts with God only as far as the heart goes along with it. Like a child running to his father, he cries to God to save him. He means saving him from his sins, temptations and everything that stands in his way, so he can obey God. His promise to obey is not boasting. It is a humble plea.

He gets up before dawn to cry out to God. He starts the day with prayer, before any business. His hope in God's word keeps him praying, even when the answer is slow. If our first thoughts in the morning are of God, they help keep us close to Him all day.
